t: Five Men of Character Who Shaped History
q: In our modern times, popular culture tends to celebrate image and self-expression. For this reason one might assume that greatness is about doing what is best for oneself. However, if we step back and study the great men in history, we will get a different idea of greatness.

Marcus Aurelius ruled the Roman Empire during one of its most turbulent periods. His time was marked by foreign wars, internal instability, and a devastating plague. Although he held absolute power, he regarded his authority as a burden that demanded character and restraint.

William Wilberforce moved easily within Britain's political and social elite. After a profound moral awakening, he dedicated his life to ending the British slave trade. For more than forty years, Wilberforce faced ridicule and fierce opposition.

While some men would have crumbled, Shackleton devoted himself entirely to his men by maintaining morale and enforcing discipline. Against the odds, he did not lose a single man on the journey and all were rescued.

The men who shaped our world were often those who accepted responsibility willingly and served others before themselves. Character is not a relic of the past. t: Expertise: The Best Professional Investment You Can Make
q: The most resilient thing you can build for yourself as a professional educator isn't a beautiful classroom (those can get reassigned) or an iron-clad curriculum (we've seen how quickly the winds of policy can reduce these to rubble) or a foolproof methodology (looking at you, AI).

it's not "all about the kids" — it's both narrower and broader than that. Narrower in the sense that it's all about advancing the long-term flourishing of young people by teaching them toward mastery. Broader in that to achieve the goal, I need to attend not just to their long-term flourishing but also to mine.

you start asking the next obvious questions: how can classes or schools or grade levels like mine best support the long-term flourishing via growth toward mastery of young people? All answers must be tested. These are the places to be rigorous.
Over time, you identify a few key answers to the question of long-term flourishing in our setting, and you resolve to dig deeper and deeper into them, year after year.

What I like about this list is that it's manageable. I don't need to blow things up to get better at any of these. I can weave this stuff in to any subject, any curriculum, any setting. And I also appreciate that, over a decade later, I'm still learning loads each year about how they work, how to improve, how to be more productive and humane.
